title: My family
title_target: Η οικογένειά μου — Ee ee-koh-yeh-nee-ah moo
goal: Name family members and say who owns what — with a possessive that stands after its noun and sometimes forces that noun to carry two accent marks at once.
bekal: use μου, σου, του, της, μας, σας, τους
keep the article in front of the possessed noun
write the second accent on certain words
ask a third person's name with Πώς τον λένε;

dialogs.title: ΔΙΑΛΟΓΟΣ — Family photos
dialogs.intro: Eleni finds Ana looking at photos on her phone. Notice that the possessive always comes **after** the noun, and that the noun keeps its article.

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: Yes, my family. This is my father.
lines.literal: yes, the — family — my. this (masc.) — he-is — the — father — my.

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: His name is Bambang. He's a teacher at a school.
lines.literal: him — they-call — Bambang. he-is — teacher — at — a — school.

lines.speaker: Ελένη:
lines.literal: and — this (fem.) — she-is — the — mother — your?

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: Yes. Her name is Siti. She works at a hospital.
lines.literal: yes. the — name — her — it-is — Siti. she-works — at — hospital.

lines.speaker: Ελένη:
lines.id: She's very pretty! And these kids?

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: Those are my cousins. Their house is next to ours.
lines.literal: these (neut. pl.) — they-are — the — cousins — my. the — house — their — it-is — next — to-the — own — our.

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: Yes. I miss them a lot.

lines.speaker: Ελένη:
lines.id: I understand. Family is everything to us.

notes: **The possessive stands AFTER the noun, and the noun keeps its article.** *το σπίτι **μου*** — literally "the house of-me". ⚠️ Two equally common mistakes: putting it in front, English-style (*μου το σπίτι*, wrong), and dropping the article (*σπίτι μου*, only right in forms of address such as *παιδί μου*).

**Great news: the possessive never changes to match the noun.** μου stays μου for masculine, feminine, neuter, singular, and plural: ο φίλος μου, η φίλη μου, το σπίτι μου, τα βιβλία μου — just like English "my". If you've ever wrestled with Italian *mio/mia/miei*, Greek is much kinder here.

⚠️ **The second accent: το όνομ**ά** μου.** If a noun is stressed on the third syllable from the end (**ό**-νο-μα, **οι**-κο-γέ-νει-α), attaching a possessive forces it to grow an extra accent on its last syllable: **το όνομά μου**, **η οικογένειά μου**, **το αυτοκίνητό του**, **ο δάσκαλός μας**. The rule: Greek doesn't allow the stress further back than the third syllable from the end, and the possessive counts as part of the word.

**Words stressed on the second-to-last or last syllable are unaffected:** το σπίτι μου, ο φίλος μου, η μητέρα μου — all keep one accent. So the second accent concerns only one group of words, and that group is easy to spot: look for an accent sitting far back.

**Πώς τον λένε; = "what's his name?"**, **Πώς τη λένε;** for a woman, **Πώς σε λένε;** for you, **Πώς σας λένε;** for you (polite). The pattern is exactly like *Με λένε* from Unit 1: literally "how do they call him".

**Δικός μου, δική μου, δικό μου = a stand-alone "mine".** Used when the noun isn't repeated, or for emphasis: *Το σπίτι **το δικό μου** είναι μικρό.* / *Δίπλα στο **δικό μας**.* ⚠️ Unlike plain μου, δικός **does** change with the gender of the noun.

**Μου λείπουν** literally means "they are missing to me" and means "I miss them". You'll fully unpack this reversed pattern in Unit 17 — for now, learn its two forms: *Μου λείπεις* (I miss you) and *Μου λείπουν* (I miss them).
**Ο μπαμπάς and η μαμά are casual; ο πατέρας and η μητέρα somewhat formal.** Greek adults keep calling their parents μπαμπά and μαμά all their lives — like "Dad" and "Mom" in English.

grammars.title: Seven possessives
body: These seven words cover the whole Greek system of possession. They're all short and cling to the word before them like a tail.
after: ⚠️ **του and της split the job like English *his* and *her*.** *το βιβλίο **του*** means "his book" — and never "her book", which must be **της**. For English speakers this is familiar ground; just remember the choice follows the owner, not the thing owned.
**The polite form uses σας**, the same as the plural: *το όνομά σας* means both "your name" (polite) and "your names".

grammars.title: When the second accent appears
body: This is the only part of the unit that really needs attention. Luckily, the rule fits in one sentence.
after: The rule: **Greek doesn't allow the stress further back than the third syllable from the end**, and the possessive counts. Since το όνομα + μου makes four syllables, the original stress falls too far back, so the word grows a backup stress at the end.

⚠️ Skipping the second accent is a **writing** mistake, not a speaking one — in speech you stress both places naturally if you follow the rhythm. If you don't write much yet, don't spend time on this now; just recognize it when you see it.

blocks.title: Three things about Greek names
items: **Greek names repeat across generations by an almost fixed rule**: the first son is named after his paternal grandfather, the first daughter after her paternal grandmother. As a result, one extended family can have four people called Γιώργος. Nicknames sort out the rest.

**Ημέρα ονόματος — the name day — matters more than the birthday.** Every Greek name is tied to a saint's day, and on that day the person receives **Χρόνια πολλά** (*KHROH-nyah poh-LAH*, "many years") from everyone they know. The same wish is used for birthdays, Christmas, and New Year.

⚠️ **Άντρας means "man" and "husband", γυναίκα means "woman" and "wife".** Only the possessive tells them apart: *μια γυναίκα* = a woman, *η γυναίκα μου* = my wife. French *femme* and German *Frau* work the same way.

Put the words in the right order.
